title: Act 5: The City of Diamonds Sold in the Street

beats.text: The empire was called *Vijayanagara*, founded in *1336*,
and its capital sat among enormous boulder fields in southern India at a place now called *Hampi*.
I want to give you the descriptions from people who actually went there,
because they don't sound real.
A Persian ambassador, *Abdur Razzaq*, arrived in the *1440s*
and reported that he had seen nothing like it anywhere on Earth.
He described bazaars where jewellers sold *pearls*, *rubies*, *emeralds* and *diamonds*
openly in the market, out on display, *the way you'd sell vegetables*.
Later, a Portuguese visitor named *Domingo Paes* described rose sellers at every corner of the city,
because people there simply could not get through a day without fresh roses.
Fresh roses. Every single day. As a *basic necessity*.
The empire ran on trade, exporting *cotton*, *spices* and *iron*,
and importing *warhorses by the thousand* from Arabia.
At its height the capital may have held several hundred thousand people,
which would have made it one of the largest cities in the world at the time.
Second only to *Beijing* by some estimates.
It lasted for a bit over two centuries, mostly by playing its neighbours off each other.
The problem with playing your neighbours off each other is that eventually your neighbours *have a conversation*.
In *1565*, *five neighbouring sultanates* put aside their own rivalries,
combined their armies, and met Vijayanagara at *Talikota*.
The empire's commander was cut down, his army broke,
and the victorious armies walked into the undefended capital.
They didn't loot it for a day. They stayed *for months*,
systematically dismantling one of the wealthiest cities on the planet.
What's left at Hampi today is about *41 square kilometres* of ruined temples, stone chariots and empty market streets,
beats.fix: Script said about 25 km². UNESCO / Wikipedia: the site covers about 41.5 km².

beats.text: and you can walk through them right now.
Meanwhile, about *2,000 kilometres* north, a young man in *Kabul* was having a miserable decade.
He had inherited a small kingdom at eleven, lost it, taken it back, lost it again,
and was now broke and out of options.
He was also the great-great-great-grandson of *Timur*, and on his mother's side, a descendant of *Genghis Khan*.
And he had *gunpowder*.

title: Act 6: The Homesick Conqueror Who Complained About the Fruit

beats.text: His name was *Babur*, and in *1526* he brought about *12,000 men* down into India
to fight the Sultan of Delhi, who had somewhere around *100,000* and a hundred war elephants.
He won in *a single morning*.
At the First Battle of *Panipat*, Babur chained his supply carts together into a long barrier,
put matchlock gunners behind them, and hid field cannons in the gaps.
Then he let the enemy charge into it.
War elephants, it turns out, do not react well to *artillery*.
They panicked and stampeded backwards through their own infantry.
That morning created the *Mughal Empire*, which would run most of the subcontinent for the next two hundred years.
And what did the founder of the greatest empire in Indian history think of India?
He wrote it down in his diary, and honestly, it's one of my favourite documents in all of history,
because the man is *relentlessly negative*.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Your Majesty, you rule Hindustan. The richest land on Earth.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: There's no ice.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: ...Sir?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: No ice. No cold water. In Kabul you could have snow in your cup.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: We have the wealth of a continent.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: The melons are bad.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Sir.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: There are no good melons. No good grapes.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: The horses are bad. The bread is bad.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Would you like to list anything positive?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: There's a great deal of gold.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: There we go.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: And absolutely nothing worth spending it on.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Shall I send for a melon?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: From Kabul.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: That's four months away, sir.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I'll wait.
Babur died four years later.
His son *Humayun* promptly lost the whole empire to an Afghan rival,
spent fifteen years in exile, got it back,
and then in *1556* died by falling down his own library stairs.
Which handed the empire to a *thirteen-year-old boy*.
And that boy turned out to be one of the most remarkable rulers anyone has ever produced.
His name was *Akbar*, and he ruled for *forty-nine years*.
He was almost certainly illiterate, possibly dyslexic, and never learned to read.
So he had books read aloud to him, constantly, for decades,
and built one of the great libraries of the world for a man who couldn't use it.
What he actually did was *harder than conquest*.
He ran a Muslim empire over a mostly Hindu population, and instead of ruling against that, he built around it.
He abolished the *jizya*, the tax non-Muslims had to pay.
He married Rajput princesses and, crucially, brought their families into his government
as *generals and governors* rather than servants. He put Hindus in the highest offices in the land.
Then he went further and started inviting Hindu, Jain, Christian, Zoroastrian and Muslim scholars into a hall
to argue theology in front of him, week after week, while he sat and listened.
His grandson had different priorities.
He would spend *twenty-two years* and a fortune building a tomb for his wife.

title: Act 7: A Billion Dollars of Marble and the Son Who Watched It from a Cell

beats.text: Shah Jahan's wife *Mumtaz Mahal* died in *1631* giving birth to their fourteenth child.
He built her the *Taj Mahal*.
Around *20,000 workers*. *Twenty-two years*.
White marble hauled by a reported *thousand elephants*,
*jade* from China, *turquoise* from Tibet, *lapis lazuli* from Afghanistan.
Modern estimates of the cost, adjusted forward, tend to land somewhere around *a billion dollars*.
For a *grave*.
And here's the detail that gets me. It's not just pretty, it's *mathematically obsessive*.
The four minarets lean very slightly outward,
so that in an earthquake they would fall away from the tomb rather than onto it.
Someone thought about that in the *1640s*.
He also commissioned the *Peacock Throne*, a solid gold seat encrusted with emeralds, rubies and diamonds,
including the *Koh-i-Noor*.
It took seven years to make and reportedly cost about *twice as much as the Taj Mahal*.
Remember it. It's *leaving the country shortly*.
Then in *1657* Shah Jahan got sick, and his four sons did what Mughal sons did,
which was fight each other to the death over the throne.
The winner was his third son, *Aurangzeb*, who executed his eldest brother, hunted down the other two,
and then made a decision that tells you everything.
He didn't kill his father. He locked him in the fort at *Agra* for the last eight years of his life,
in a room with a view of the Taj Mahal across the river.
Aurangzeb ruled for *forty-nine years* and pushed the Mughal Empire to its *largest size ever*.
Look at this map. Almost the entire subcontinent under one flag, for the only time before the British.
It was also the beginning of the end, for *two reasons*.
The first was policy. He reversed Akbar's approach, brought back the *jizya* tax on non-Muslims,
and took a harder religious line. In an empire where the overwhelming majority of his subjects were Hindu,
that turned a lot of *quiet regions loud*.
The second was the *Deccan*. He went south to finish off his enemies
and spent the last *twenty-seven years* of his life down there, campaigning.
He won battles constantly and never won the war, because his main opponents didn't fight wars the way he did.
They were *Marathas*, the movement founded by a man named *Shivaji*,
beats.fix: Script said the Marathas were 'led by' Shivaji during this campaign, but Shivaji died in 1680; the 1681–1707 war was fought by his successors.

beats.text: and they specialised in fast cavalry raids, hill forts, and *vanishing*.
Aurangzeb died in *1707* at eighty-eight, in a tent, in the Deccan, having drained the richest treasury in the world.
He left instructions that his own burial be paid for out of money he'd earned personally copying manuscripts.
Thirty-two years later, a *Persian king* would walk into Delhi and take everything that was left.
